# 2 Corinthians 8 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

**Background (whole chapter):** Chapters 8–9 form a unit on the collection for the poor saints in Jerusalem. Paul had previously given instructions about this collection in 1 Corinthians 16:1–4, but the Corinthians' falling out with Paul had stalled it. Now that reconciliation has occurred (ch. 7), Paul reengages the topic. The key Greek word is *charis* ("grace"), used 10 times across chapters 8–9, framing giving itself as a work of God's grace.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-8-commentary
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm

---

## v. 1: "Now, brothers, we want you to know about the grace that God has given the churches of Macedonia."

**Traditional reading:** Paul opens by calling the generosity of the Macedonian churches "the grace of God." The giving itself is a gift from God, not merely a human decision. Paul uses the tender address "brothers," signaling that the earlier rift has been healed. The "grace of God" here means both the disposition to give generously and the actual collection itself — God is the source, and the Macedonians are the instruments. The verb "given" is in the perfect tense, signifying a past act with continuing effects. Gill notes that this liberality is called "the grace of God" because it springs from grace, is assisted by grace, and has the love and favour of God as its motive. The churches of Macedonia included Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-8-commentary
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/

---

## v. 2: "In the terrible ordeal they suffered, their abundant joy and deep poverty overflowed into rich generosity."

**Traditional reading:** The Macedonians endured both external persecution ("a great trial of affliction") and extreme poverty. The Romans had confiscated much Macedonian wealth after conquest. Yet their joy in Christ — not their circumstances — was the spring of their generosity. Ellicott observes that the "abundance of their joy" refers to cheerfulness in giving, not merely joy amid trials. The phrase "deep poverty" (Greek: *kata bathous ptocheia*) means poverty down to the depths — utter destitution. Despite this, they gave with "rich generosity." The Greek word for "generosity" (*haplotēs*) literally means "singleness" or "simplicity" of heart, which when expressed in giving becomes liberality. Giving is measured by sacrifice, not amount — a principle illustrated by the widow's mite (Mark 12:42–44; Luke 21:1–4).

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-8-commentary

**Piper (Reformed Baptist):** The grace of God had filled the Macedonians with an abundance of joy, and that joy overflowed in generosity. "Love is the overflow of joy in God which meets the needs of others." The Macedonians' giving was not obligation-driven but joy-driven — they were pursuing a greater joy in giving than in keeping.

— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/finding-joy-through-loving-others-with-portuguese-interpretation
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/christmas-joy-vs-the-kirchensteuer

---

## v. 3: "For I testify that they gave according to their ability and even beyond it. Of their own accord,"

**Traditional reading:** Paul "bears witness" (*martyreō*) — he takes the stand as one giving legal testimony — to three things: (1) they gave according to their ability (proportional giving); (2) they gave beyond their ability (sacrificial giving — their willingness outstripped their resources); (3) they gave of their own accord (*authairetos*), meaning voluntarily, without coercion or pressure. Gill notes that they did not actually give beyond their power (no one can), but their hearts were larger than their purses; they were willing beyond their ability. MacArthur (Baptist) emphasizes that freewill giving has always been God's plan and should not be confused with tithing, which was Israel's national taxation system.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-8-commentary
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/

---

## v. 4: "they earnestly pleaded with us for the privilege of sharing in this service to the saints."

**Traditional reading:** The Macedonians did not wait to be asked — they begged (*deomenoi*, "imploring with much urgency") Paul to receive their gift. Ellicott notes the Greek literally reads "asking of us the grace (or favour) and fellowship in the ministry of the saints" — they considered it a *privilege* to participate. This reverses the normal dynamic: normally the fundraiser begs the donor; here the donors begged the fundraiser. The word "fellowship" (*koinōnia*) indicates that giving creates a bond between giver and recipient.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/

**Piper (Reformed Baptist):** The Macedonians "begged for the privilege of giving more money." They were not acting out of obligation but out of desire — like children begging to ride a roller coaster again. This shows that self-denial in giving is actually the pursuit of a greater joy.

— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/finding-joy-through-loving-others-with-portuguese-interpretation

---

## v. 5: "And not only did they do as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then to us, because it was the will of God."

**Traditional reading:** This verse is widely regarded as the key to the entire passage. The Macedonians exceeded Paul's hopes not merely in the amount given but in the order of their giving: first themselves to the Lord, then their resources to Paul (as Christ's agent). Gill explains that "gave their own selves to the Lord" refers to their initial conversion — they entrusted their souls to Christ for salvation and submitted to His rule. Only after this total self-surrender did material giving flow naturally. "By the will of God" indicates that even this self-giving was enabled by divine grace, not human effort. Enduring Word (Guzik) states: "If we really give ourselves to the Lord, then the right kind of material giving will naturally follow."

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-8-commentary

---

## v. 6: "So we urged Titus to help complete your act of grace, just as he had started it."

**Traditional reading:** Following the Macedonians' example, Paul urged (*parakaleō*) Titus to return to Corinth and bring the collection to completion. Titus had previously begun the collection during an earlier visit. Gill notes that the Macedonians themselves may have joined in urging Titus to go — the Vulgate, Syriac, and Arabic versions read it this way. "This grace" (the collection) needed to be finished; good intentions without follow-through are worthless.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-8-commentary

---

## v. 7: "But just as you excel in everything—in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in complete earnestness, and in the love we inspired in you—see that you also excel in this grace of giving."

**Traditional reading:** Paul may be using a touch of holy sarcasm here: the Corinthians prided themselves on excelling in spiritual gifts. He lists five areas of supposed excellence — faith, speech (utterance), knowledge, earnestness (diligence), and love. Ellicott observes that Paul dexterously combines the gifts of "utterance and knowledge" (which he acknowledged in 1 Corinthians 1:5) with the "earnestness and love" he has spoken of in this very epistle. Then he challenges them: add "this grace also" — financial giving — to the list. Gill comments that to excel in one grace but not another is not praiseworthy. MacArthur (via Precept Austin) summarizes: giving should be in harmony with other Christian virtues already recognized in them.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-8-commentary
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/

**Note on the textual variant:** Some manuscripts read "the love we inspired in you" (your love for us), while others read "our love for you." Ellicott notes the reading "your love to us" has abundant authority and better suits Paul's purpose of praising them for something actually theirs.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm

---

## v. 8: "I am not making a demand, but I am testing the sincerity of your love in comparison to the earnestness of others."

**Traditional reading:** Paul explicitly disclaims commanding them. Ellicott notes the ambiguity: is Paul disclaiming a tone of command, or the sanction of divine authority? He leans toward the former but says ultimately the two merge — Paul gives no commands because he has received no commandment from the Lord on this specific matter (cf. 1 Corinthians 7:6, 12, 25). Instead, Paul is "testing" (*dokimazō*) — a word that means testing with the expectation of proving genuineness. The test is whether their love is sincere, using the Macedonians' earnestness as the comparison point. Gill says Paul was moved by the generous example of others, seeking "a proof of their sincere love and affection to the Lord, and to his people."

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/

**Piper (Reformed Baptist):** Paul "very consciously avoids commanding the people to give. The reason is because he wants the giving to be a proof of love." Forced giving is taxation, not love. He connects this to 1 Corinthians 13:3 — giving without love profits nothing. Piper ties this to his rejection of the German church tax (Kirchensteuer) as incompatible with biblical giving.

— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/christmas-joy-vs-the-kirchensteuer

**MacArthur (Baptist):** Giving is a test of love's sincerity. Freewill, grace-motivated giving — not tithing as obligation — is the NT pattern.

— https://www.gty.org/sermons/47-59/the-poverty-that-made-us-rich (via search excerpt)

---

## v. 9: "For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich."

**Traditional reading:** This is the theological high point. The ultimate example of grace-giving is Christ Himself. "Though He was rich" points to Christ's pre-incarnate divine glory — the eternal Son sharing the riches of heaven (Psalm 45:8). "He became poor" refers to His incarnation and earthly life of humility, culminating in the cross. Ellicott notes this echoes Philippians 2:6–7 ("He emptied Himself") and adds that Jesus also chose outward poverty — He had nowhere to lay His head (Matthew 8:20), lived as one who could be called a beggar (the Greek *ptōcheia* is the word for beggary in Luke 16:20–22). Yet He "added" poverty without losing divine riches inwardly. The purpose: "that you through His poverty might become rich" — not materially rich but spiritually rich with salvation, joy, and eternal inheritance.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm

**MacArthur (Baptist):** Emphasizes that Christ's giving was "grace giving" — not duty, not obligation, not a fixed percentage. It was spontaneous and from the heart. Christ's poverty purchased our spiritual riches.

— https://www.gty.org/sermons/47-59/the-poverty-that-made-us-rich (via excerpt)

**Piper (Reformed Baptist):** Christ's riches were infinite — He existed as the glorious second person of the Trinity. His condescension to be born in a cattle stall and die on a criminal's cross was "the unimaginable condescension." Through His poverty we become rich — "not rich in money, but… rich in joy and rich in liberality, and… rich in love."

— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/christmas-joy-vs-the-kirchensteuer

**On the "become rich" phrase:** No traditional commentator I found reads this as promising material wealth. All agree it means spiritual riches. This stands against prosperity-gospel interpretations (see separate note below).

---

## v. 10: "And this is my opinion about what is helpful for you in this matter: Last year you were the first not only to give, but even to have such a desire."

**Traditional reading:** Paul carefully distinguishes his "opinion" (*gnōmē*) from a command (as in 1 Corinthians 7:25). He reminds the Corinthians they were actually ahead of the Macedonians — they were first both in desiring to give and in beginning to do so, "a year ago." Ellicott explains the time reference: if Paul wrote around autumn and the Corinthians began collecting around the previous Easter (per 1 Corinthians 16:1–2), a Jewish reckoning of the year (beginning with Tishri, September/October) would place that in "last year" even if less than twelve months had passed. The point is to stir honorable competition: the Corinthians started first; they should not now be outdone.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/

---

## v. 11: "Now finish the work, so that you may complete it just as eagerly as you began, according to your means."

**Traditional reading:** Paul identifies three stages: (1) the readiness to will, (2) the beginning of the doing, and (3) now the completing. Ellicott notes the progression: "complete the doing" — the Corinthians had the desire and had started, but the work remained unfinished. "According to your means" (literally "out of what you have") ties the completion to their actual resources. Gill adds that the rule and measure of giving is "out of their own, what they were possessed of, and according to their ability."

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/

---

## v. 12: "For if the eagerness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what he does not have."

**Traditional reading:** God measures giving by the willingness of the heart, not the size of the gift. "If there is first a willing mind" — the Greek *prothymia* means eagerness, readiness. The gift is "acceptable" (*euprosdektos*) to God when given from a willing heart, in proportion to what one possesses. God does not ask for what we do not have. Ellicott notes that the widow's mite story (Luke 21:1–4), found in the Gospel of Luke (Paul's companion), was likely known to Paul. Enduring Word (Guzik) states: "True Christian giving cannot be measured by the amount. One might give a million dollars and yet not give enough; another may give one dollar and give with tremendous sacrifice and generosity."

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm

---

## v. 13: "It is not our intention that others may be relieved while you are burdened, but that there may be equality."

**Traditional reading:** Paul clarifies that he is not trying to impoverish Corinth to enrich Jerusalem. The goal is not to make others "eased" (*anesis*, relieved) while the Corinthians are "burdened" (*thlipsis*, afflicted). Ellicott sees this as Paul answering the "charity begins at home" objection that was apparently circulating in Corinth. Calvin (quoted by Enduring Word) says this refutes "fanatics who think that you have done nothing unless you strip yourself completely and put everything into a common fund."

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/

---

## v. 14: "At the present time, your surplus will meet their need, so that in turn their surplus will meet your need. Then there will be equality."

**Traditional reading:** Paul envisions mutual exchange — not one-way charity. Now the Corinthians' material abundance supplies Jerusalem's material lack. In the future, Jerusalem's spiritual abundance (or possibly future material abundance, if conditions change) would supply Corinth's need. Ellicott explicitly rejects the Roman Catholic reading (found in Estius and others) that this verse teaches a "transfer of superfluous merits" from the poor to the rich at the day of judgment. The equality is practical mutual care within the body of Christ. Hodge (quoted by Enduring Word) notes Scripture avoids both "the injustice and destructive evils of agrarian communism" (by recognizing property rights and making almsgiving optional) and "the heartless disregard of the poor" (by inculcating universal brotherhood).

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/

---

## v. 15: "As it is written: 'He who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall.'"

**Traditional reading:** Paul quotes Exodus 16:18 (the gathering of manna). The manna — God's provision in the wilderness — illustrates that in God's economy, hoarding fails and sharing meets needs. Those who gathered more shared with those who gathered less, and all had enough. Ellicott notes Paul quotes the LXX version. Hodge: "Property is like manna, it will not bear hoarding." Calvin adds: "Just as manna, which was hoarded to excess out of greed or lack of faith, immediately putrefied, so we should have no doubt that riches which are heaped up at the expense of our brethren are accursed."

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm

---

## v. 16: "But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same devotion I have for you."

**Traditional reading:** Paul shifts from exhortation to commendation of the messengers who will collect the gift. He thanks God (not Titus's natural character) for putting the same earnest care (*spoudē*) for the Corinthians into Titus's heart. Ellicott notes the verb "putteth" is present tense — God was presently working this care in Titus. "The same earnest care" means the same care Paul himself had.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm

---

## v. 17: "For not only did he welcome our appeal, but he is eagerly coming to you of his own volition."

**Traditional reading:** Titus both responded positively to Paul's urging and exceeded it — he was coming eagerly on his own initiative. Ellicott explains "he went" is an epistolary aorist: Titus was about to depart as the bearer of this very letter. This gives the Corinthians double assurance: Titus comes with apostolic authority *and* with personal enthusiasm.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm

---

## v. 18: "Along with Titus we are sending the brother who is praised by all the churches for his work in the gospel."

**Traditional reading:** The identity of this unnamed brother is uncertain. Ellicott surveys the options: patristic tradition (reflected in the Church of England's Collect for St. Luke's Day) favoured Luke, and Ellicott himself argues this is the strongest candidate — Luke was a preacher at Antioch, Troas, and Philippi; his Gospel emphasises the danger of riches and the blessedness of almsgiving; and his influence is traceable in the liberal giving at Philippi. Other suggestions include Tychicus, Trophimus, Mark, or Gaius, but Ellicott finds less evidence for these. Gill adds that this person was "of note and fame in all the churches."

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm

---

## v. 19: "More than that, this brother was chosen by the churches to accompany us with the offering—the gracious gift we administer to honor the Lord Himself and to show our eagerness to help."

**Traditional reading:** The brother was not appointed by Paul alone but "chosen" (*cheirotoneō*) by the churches — Ellicott says this implies a definite appointment by popular election of the Macedonian churches. This ensured democratic accountability. The purpose was twofold: (1) to glorify the Lord, and (2) to demonstrate the Corinthians' "ready mind" (eagerness). The collection is again called "this grace" (*charis*).

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm

---

## v. 20: "We hope to avoid any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift."

**Traditional reading:** Paul took deliberate precautions against accusations of financial impropriety. By sending multiple trusted, church-appointed delegates, he ensured the collection would be handled transparently. Gill comments that "more persons than one were sent, was to prevent any suspicion of converting the collections to wrong purposes." Ellicott notes the Greek word translated "abundance" (*hadrotēs*, literally "succulence" or "fullness") is unique in the NT and may reflect Luke's medical vocabulary (used by Hippocrates).

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm

---

## v. 21: "For we are taking great care to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord, but also in the eyes of men."

**Traditional reading:** Paul quotes or alludes to Proverbs 3:4 (LXX): "Provide things honest in the sight of God and man." Ellicott notes: "The citation is interesting, as showing that even one who was taught by the Spirit, as St. Paul was, could yet find guidance for his daily conduct in a book which seems to many almost to be below the level of the spiritual life." Paul's point: even though his own conscience was clear before God, he insisted on accountability before human observers because men might suspect him. Financial integrity in ministry requires transparency before both God and people.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/

---

## v. 22: "And we are sending along with them our brother whose earnestness has been proven many times and in many ways, and now even more so by his great confidence in you."

**Traditional reading:** A third, also unnamed brother is sent. Ellicott considers Tychicus the most likely candidate (he went with Paul to Jerusalem per Acts 20:4, and the commendations in Ephesians 6:21 and Colossians 4:7 match the language here). Clement of Rome is also a possibility (Philippians 4:3). This brother had been "proven" (*dokimazō*) diligent in many situations, and his confidence in the Corinthians made him even more eager for this mission.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm

---

## v. 23: "As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker among you. As for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, to the glory of Christ."

**Traditional reading:** Paul gives a final commendation. Titus is his *koinōnos* (partner, sharer) and *synergos* (fellow-worker) — terms of deep collegiality. The two unnamed brothers are "messengers of the churches" — the Greek word is *apostoloi* ("apostles"), used here (as in Philippians 2:25) in the lower sense of "delegates" or "sent ones" of the churches, not in the sense of the Twelve. Ellicott adds a striking note on "the glory of Christ": these men not only work for Christ's glory but actually reflect His glory in their character — "You may see that glory in them" (connecting to 2 Corinthians 3:18).

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm

---

## v. 24: "In full view of the churches, then, show these men the proof of your love and the reason for our boasting about you."

**Traditional reading:** Paul's final appeal uses every legitimate motivational lever: (1) the watching eyes of the Macedonian churches, (2) the need to prove their love for Paul, and (3) the need to validate Paul's boasting about them (elaborated in 9:2). Ellicott: "With a subtle knowledge of human nature, he attacks them, as it were, on every side. They have to compete with Macedonia; they have to show their love for their teacher; they have to sustain their own reputation." Gill concludes that they should "make it appear that he had not boasted of them in vain."

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/8.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### On Tithing vs. Freewill Giving

The chapter says nothing about tithing — the collection is a special one-time offering, not regular temple tax. This has led to differing applications:

- **Baptist/Reformed (MacArthur, GTY):** MacArthur explicitly states that "freewill giving is not to be confused with tithing, which related to the national taxation system of Israel… and is paralleled in the NT and present by paying taxes." Giving should be freewill, grace-motivated, not a fixed percentage.
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-8-commentary (citing MacArthur Study Bible)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik):** Guzik holds a middle position: the tithe (10%) is "a good principle for giving and perhaps a broad benchmark," yet the NT "nowhere specifically commands tithing." For some, 10% is not nearly enough; for others, 5% may be a massive step of faith. What matters is proportion, willingness, and sacrifice, not a fixed percentage.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-8/

- **Reformed Baptist (Piper, Desiring God):** Piper emphasizes that commanded giving is not giving at all — it is taxation. Giving must flow from joy, not compulsion. He specifically rejected the German church tax system as incompatible with 2 Corinthians 8.
  — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/christmas-joy-vs-the-kirchensteuer

### On v. 9 and the "Prosperity Gospel"

No source I examined reads "that you through His poverty might become rich" as a promise of material wealth. All traditional commentators — Baptist, Reformed, Pentecostal, Anglican — read it as spiritual riches: salvation, joy, liberality, and eternal inheritance. This chapter is sometimes cited by prosperity-gospel teachers to claim that Jesus' atonement guarantees financial wealth, but that interpretation finds no support among the sources searched. The "riches" are consistently understood as spiritual.

---

## Other Views

### Roman Catholic Reading of v. 14 (the "transfer of merits")

Ellicott notes that Roman Catholic commentators (such as Estius) have read verse 14 as teaching that the rich give material alms to the poor, and in exchange the poor transfer their "superfluous merits" to the rich, especially at the hour of death and the day of judgment. Ellicott firmly rejects this: "It is reading too much between the lines… controversial ingenuity is 'capable of anything.'" He insists the passage speaks only of mutual material and spiritual fellowship, not a treasury of merits.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/8.htm
